Good to be out of debt and have some money in the bank; you should set up an official emergency fund and then look to start investing. These are the steps in order that I recommend in general.

Solid goals are:  
- Get out of debt  
- Create/increase an emergency fund. Basic is 3 months of minimal spending, longer goal of 6 months of normal spending  
- Save for retirement  
- Save for the long term (house/early retirement)  

Automated payments - you can set up online or in the bank a monthly automated payment for almost all debt and savings.

1. Set up a separate emergency fund. Put these funds into a tax-free savings account. If you already maximize your contributions for other reasons, put the emergency fund into a regular (non-registered) account.

2. If you have a job with a matching retirement plan or similar, maximize the match as long as you can work on high-interest debt or contribute to your basic emergency fund.

3. If you have debt over 10% interest, pay it off now! Pay as much as you can each month. Use the mantra "I cannot afford it." Put your credit card away until it has a 0 balance.

4. Contribute something to your basic emergency fund if it is not already big enough: 3 months of minimal spending. Determine how much more you need in the emergency fund, divide it by 12 (or less), and put that much into the emergency fund each month.

5. If you have debt from 7-10% interest, focus on paying it off but make sure to contribute something to your basic emergency fund. Focus less and less as the interest rate is below 7%.

6. If you have debt less than 3% interest, pay it on schedule - do not overpay.

7. Contribute everything else to your basic emergency fund: 3 months of minimal spending. If the basic emergency fund is big enough, contribute something to the ultimate emergency fund: 6 months of normal spending.

8. After all of the above is covered, focus on maximizing your tax-free savings account contributions.

9. After the tax-free savings account is maximized, maximize retirement account contributions (deducting any contributions & match from #1).

10. If you have a mortgage or are buying a home, save to get at least 20% down and plan and set up to overpay by at least 10% per month.

I agree that the ecosystem is immature. There are four parts that make up a decentralized digital currency.    

First is the protocol specification itself, from the original whitepaper to all of the improvement proposals implemented and other components. Everything else stems from the specification.  

Second, there are the software developers focused on mining. These individuals create software applications that can be run to generate the blockchain. All blocks (and thus the digital currency) stem from those software applications.  

Third, there are the miners. These are the individuals who take the mining software of their choice and run it to compete and create the blockchain and thus the digital currency.  

Fourth and finally, there is the ecosystem - everyone and everything else. These are the individuals and systems that will take the miners' created digital currency, pay money and services for them so the miners can pay their bills and profit. The ecosystem then uses the digital currency as a medium of exchange/payment system/alternative currency/gambling platform/etc.  

Now to generalize and categorize, in my humble opinion...  
On one side, the group advocating for a specific upgrade includes many core developers (an important subset of some of the mining software developers) and a few large organizations from the ecosystem who want to implement a particular solution to increase the speed of transactions and the number of transactions possible indirectly (more transactions can happen off-chain).  

On the other side, the group supporting an alternative approach consists of a small number of developers, quite a few miners, and a large portion of the ecosystem that simply wants to increase the maximum block size, thus increasing the number of transactions possible.  

So we have two competing camps with code that is (or close to being) ready to run.  
Who gets to decide what's in the decentralized digital currency? In this case, the miners. The miners will choose the software that is in their best interest to maximize value to themselves - likely through self-interest (we profit more with/without the proposed upgrade or small/large blocks), their perspective on the overall value of the digital currency system (more people will use it if we choose option X), or some political reason (we dislike individual X!).  

If the majority of miners adopt one or the other proposed option, most of the ecosystem would willingly, apathetically, or grudgingly follow.

Most mutual funds are "open ended" - any number of units can exist as demand requires. For your standard stock/bond mutual funds, the mutual fund holds underlying assets and that value is divided across all units. The price of a mutual fund is the Net Asset Value (NAV). Add up the value of all stocks and bonds divided by the number of units = Net Asset Value.

Theoretically, when you buy mutual fund units, the units are created and need to be backed by the appropriate amount of underlying assets - your money is used to fund the purchase of those assets. Similarly, when you sell, the units are destroyed and the underlying assets should be sold to provide you the money back.

In reality, since mutual fund units usually can only be bought/sold once a day, the buy/sell totals for a day roughly even out each day so the mutual fund only buys/sells the small delta on the open market or holds a separate small "float" of investments that make up the mutual fund.

ETFs are a little different. Basically, one company is the ETF fund sponsor and manages creating/destroying ETF units with specific rules. Other large companies that are Authorized Participants can deliver to the Sponsor a specific group and number of assets in the ETF (e.g., 10,000 shares of each stock in a major index) and get a specific number of ETF shares (called a creation unit) that can then be sold on the open market (e.g., 50,000 ETF shares). Similarly, the Authorized Participants can provide a set number of ETF shares and redeem them for the agreed-upon number of underlying assets.

This way, if the ETF price is too high compared to the underlying assets, the authorized participants can buy the assets needed, hand them into the sponsor for ETF shares, and sell the ETF shares for a profit. The same works in reverse if the ETF price is too low.

In full reality, many of the mutual funds, ETF sponsors, and authorized participants have agreements with large institutional investors that hold a lot of an underlying asset to borrow some of the asset (for a small fee) and use that as a "float" to work with. For ETFs, shares are not physically or even electronically "shipped" to the other company, but are put into escrow accounts.

Here is some general advice for people finished with school:  

Solid goals are:  
- Get out of debt  
- Create / increase an emergency fund. Basic is 3 months minimal spending, longer goal of 6 months normal spending  
- Save for retirement

Automated payments - you can set up online or in the bank a monthly automated payment for almost all debt and savings.  

1. Set up a separate emergency fund. Put these funds into a tax-free savings account. If you already maximize your contributions for other reasons, put the emergency fund into a regular (non-registered) account.  

2. If you have a job with a matching retirement plan or similar, maximize the match as long as you can work on high-interest debt or contribute to your basic emergency fund.  

3. If you have debt over 10% interest, pay it off now! Pay as much as you can each month. Use the mantra "I cannot afford it." Put your credit card away until it has a 0 balance.  

4. Contribute something to your basic emergency fund if it is not already big enough: 3 months of minimal spending. Determine how much more you need in the emergency fund, divide it by 12 (or less), and put that much into the emergency fund each month.  

5. If you have debt from 7 - 10% interest, focus on paying it off but make sure to contribute something to your basic emergency fund. Focus less and less as the interest rate is below 7%.  

6. If you have debt less than 3% interest, pay it on schedule - do not overpay.  

7. Contribute everything else to your basic emergency fund: 3 months of minimal spending. If the basic emergency fund is big enough, contribute something to the ultimate emergency fund: 6 months of normal spending.  

8. After all of the above is covered, focus on maximizing your tax-free savings account contributions.  

9. After the tax-free savings account is maximized, maximize retirement plan contributions (deducting any contributions & match from #1).  

10. If you have a mortgage or are buying a home, save to get at least 20% down and plan and set up to overpay by at least 10% per month.

Since someone will ask, here is the rationale for Tax-Free Savings Account first:  
tl;dr: Both are good, most people will do better with a Tax-Free Savings Account.  
Both Tax-Free Savings Accounts and Registered Retirement Savings Plans are good. For years, Registered Retirement Savings Plans have been and are still great, awesome, amazing, and fantastic. Today, Tax-Free Savings Accounts are even better. Before Tax-Free Savings Accounts, the mantra has been to invest in Registered Retirement Savings Plans as it was better than a regular account. In the last 6 years, Tax-Free Savings Accounts are generally better than Registered Retirement Savings Plans - it depends on your current income, expected withdrawal income, pensions, rates of returns, etc. In the few cases where Registered Retirement Savings Plans could be better financially, they can only be better than Tax-Free Savings Accounts if you contribute the upfront tax savings that the Registered Retirement Savings Plan gets you back into the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. For example, you can contribute $3000 after-tax dollars in a year and are in a 33% tax bracket. If $3000 is deposited into a Tax-Free Savings Account, you are done. If it is deposited into a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, you will get a $1000 back in taxes, which MUST be reinvested to have any chance of beating a Tax-Free Savings Account. In fact, you should deposit $4500 into the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and get a $1500 refund to make it a net deposit of $3000. One difference of Tax-Free Savings Account vs. Registered Retirement Savings Plan is the flexibility. Flexibility is good because you can use a Tax-Free Savings Account for non-retirement purposes such as an emergency fund or saving for a car. Flexibility is bad if you are using the Tax-Free Savings Account for retirement and discipline is a challenge... it is "easier" in terms of pain and financial impact to prematurely remove funds from a Tax-Free Savings Account than a Registered Retirement Savings Plan.

Rake / vig / juice is the extra added on to every bet or slight changes to the winning odds / payouts so that the house always makes money.  

Team A 2:1 vs. Team B 1:2.  
Bet $100 on Team A & win, win $200 + $100 original.   
Bet $200 on Team B & win, win $100 + $200 original.  
$300 in bets and $300 payouts either way... to make money the house charges 10% vig on bets:  
Bet $110 on Team A & win, win $200 + $100 original.   
Bet $220 on Team B & win, win $100 + $200 original.  
$330 in bets and $300 payouts either way... house gets $30 profit guaranteed.  

In pari-mutuel all bets are put into a pot, the house takes its cut and the rest is winnings.  
e.g. 11 competitors race, each getting a single $100 bet to win.   Bets = $1100.  The house takes $100 profit.  
1 competitor wins, the pool of $1000 is given to the winner.  

In some betting systems, the odds never add up to hand out all of the money:  
11 competitors race, each with 9:1 odds.  
Each competitor has a total of $100 bet to win.  Bets = $1100.  
1 competitor wins, win $900 + $100 original.  
$1100 in bets, $1000 in payout, $100 house profit.  

The house uses the profits to provide the betting service.   The house also tries to even out the bets so its win/loss risk is not impacted by the result of the event.  
There are other systems to guarantee profit.  Think about this the next time you invest - the house always wins.

Here is some general advice for people finished with school:  

Solid goals are:  
- Get out of debt  
- Create / increase an emergency fund. Basic is 3 months minimal spending, longer goal of 6 months normal spending  
- Save for retirement  
- Save for the long term (house/early retirement)  

Automated payments - you can set up online or in the bank a monthly automated payment for almost all debt and savings.  

1. Set up a separate emergency fund. Put these funds into a tax-free savings account. If you already maximize your contributions for other reasons, put the emergency fund into a regular (non-registered) account.  

2. If you have a job with a matching retirement plan or similar, maximize the match as long as you can work on high-interest debt or contribute to your basic emergency fund.  

3. If you have debt over 10% interest, pay it off now! Pay as much as you can each month. Use the mantra "I cannot afford it." Put your credit card away until it has a 0 balance.  

4. Contribute something to your basic emergency fund if it is not already big enough: 3 months of minimal spending. Determine how much more you need in the emergency fund, divide it by 12 (or less), and put that much into the emergency fund each month.  

5. If you have debt from 7 - 10% interest, focus on paying it off but make sure to contribute something to your basic emergency fund. Focus less and less as the interest rate is below 7%.  

6. If you have debt less than 3% interest, pay it on schedule - do not overpay.  

7. Contribute everything else to your basic emergency fund: 3 months of minimal spending. If the basic emergency fund is big enough, contribute something to the ultimate emergency fund: 6 months of normal spending.  

8. After all of the above is covered, focus on maximizing your tax-free savings account contributions.  

9. After the tax-free savings account is maximized, maximize retirement plan contributions (deducting any contributions & match from #1).  

10. If you have a mortgage or are buying a home, save to get at least 20% down and plan and set up to overpay by at least 10% per month.
